title: The App That Created a Hundred Jobs

pages.text: At their JHS coding club in Accra, fourteen-year-old Kwame and Adwoa loved writing code on the school computers. One afternoon, Bakery owner Madam Akua rushed past the school gate looking stressed: her dough mixer had stopped working, and she did not know which neighbourhood electrician she could trust to fix it quickly and fairly. Meanwhile, right across the road at the vocational training centre, skilled young graduates sat waiting all week for customers to find them.
sentences: At their JHS coding club in Accra, fourteen-year-old Kwame and Adwoa loved writing code on the school computers.

One afternoon, Bakery owner Madam Akua rushed past the school gate looking stressed: her dough mixer had stopped working, and she did not know which neighbourhood electrician she could trust to fix it quickly and fairly.
Meanwhile, right across the road at the vocational training centre, skilled young graduates sat waiting all week for customers to find them.
pages.alt: Outside the school gate in Accra, Madam Akua worries over her bakery while skilled young technicians wait with their toolboxes across the street.

pages.text: ‘We can solve this in one weekend with an app!’ declared Kwame excitedly. Without interviewing a single electrician or shopkeeper, Kwame and Adwoa stayed indoors for two weeks building Version 1. They packed it with heavy animations, five pages of English registration forms, and high-resolution video uploads. Proudly, they launched it to the neighbourhood.

pages.alt: Kwame and Adwoa excitedly code a complicated, graphic-heavy app on a laptop without talking to any customers first.

pages.text: Version 1 was a complete flop! In the first week, only three people opened it, and zero repairs were booked. Why? The heavy animations ate up expensive mobile data, failed to load when the network signal dropped to 2G or 3G, and required customers to type long technical descriptions they did not understand. Kwame stared at the empty dashboard in dismay.

pages.alt: A technician’s phone shows a spinning loading circle as Kwame and Adwoa look at their empty booking dashboard in disappointment.

pages.text: ‘We built for our own laptop screen instead of listening to real people,’ said Adwoa. They closed their laptops, picked up paper notebooks, and spent a month doing customer discovery—interviewing thirty shopkeepers, parents and vocational technicians with Master Ibrahim. They learned three critical truths: users needed tiny data usage, clear upfront pricing, and a way to know every technician was genuinely qualified and safe.

pages.alt: Adwoa and Kwame interview Madam Akua and Master Ibrahim with paper notebooks, listening carefully to what they actually need.

pages.text: Years of learning and disciplined iteration followed. As they progressed through senior high and university computer science and business courses, Kwame and Adwoa rebuilt the platform from the ground up. Version 2 used ultra-light screens that loaded in two seconds on slow connections, worked via a simple USSD short-code for phones without internet data, and let customers pick common repairs with three taps.

pages.alt: Now young adults, Kwame and Adwoa test a fast, lightweight version of the platform that works on both smartphones and basic feature phones.

pages.text: Because the app handled customers’ home addresses, phone numbers and mobile-money payments, Kwame and Adwoa made cybersecurity and privacy a top priority. Following Ghana’s Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), they collected only necessary information, encrypted every user record, never sold customer data to strangers, and masked phone numbers after a job was completed.

pages.alt: Kwame implements encryption and privacy shields on the server while Adwoa reviews their Data Protection Commission compliance checklist.

pages.text: Next, they solved the hardest problem of all: human trust. An app is only as good as the people behind it! Partnering with Master Ibrahim’s technical institute, Adwoa set up a rigorous verification and training programme. Every plumber, electrician, solar installer and appliance technician passed a practical skills test, an ID and background check, and customer-service training before receiving a verified badge and uniform.

pages.alt: Master Ibrahim and Adwoa test and certify young female and male technicians in a hands-on electrical and plumbing lab.

pages.text: How did the business sustain itself financially? Kwame and Adwoa designed a transparent revenue model. When Madam Akua booked an electrical repair for one hundred cedis, ninety cedis—ninety percent—went directly to the certified technician for their skilled work and transport, while the platform kept a ten-cedi—ten percent—service fee to pay for servers, customer support, insurance and training.

pages.alt: A visual diagram shows a 100-cedi repair payment splitting cleanly into 90 cedis for the technician and 10 cedis for the platform’s operating costs.

pages.text: Growth was steady, not overnight magic. In Year 1, only twelve technicians used the platform. In Year 2, a server crash during a rainy weekend taught Kwame to build automated backups, and a dispute over a spare part taught Adwoa to add digital receipts and a thirty-day workmanship guarantee. Step by step, word of mouth spread across Accra, Kumasi, Cape Coast and Takoradi.

Step by step, word of mouth spread across Accra, Kumasi, Cape Coast and Takoradi.
pages.alt: A timeline montage shows the team fixing a server bug, issuing digital receipts and expanding steadily over five years.

pages.text: Five years after launching Version 2, Kwame and Adwoa celebrated a milestone that meant more to them than any trophy. Their company employed twenty-five full-time salaried staff—software engineers, customer-support agents, quality inspectors and accountants—and provided steady, dignified daily income for seventy-five certified independent technicians across Ghana. Twenty-five plus seventy-five equalled one hundred decent jobs!

pages.alt: Kwame, Adwoa and Master Ibrahim stand proudly with twenty-five office staff and seventy-five certified technicians in a sunny courtyard.

pages.text: One of those seventy-five technicians was twenty-two-year-old Esi, who used her steady ninety-percent earnings to rent her own workshop, enroll in a Tier 3 personal pension, and train two younger apprentices from her neighbourhood. When one business creates honest work, the ripple reaches whole families and communities.

pages.text: When Kwame and Adwoa visited their old JHS coding club to mentor the newest class of fourteen-year-olds, Adwoa wrote one sentence on the board: Code is a tool; solving human problems with fairness and trust is the business. The students opened their notebooks—ready to listen first, learn deeply, and build for Ghana’s future.

activities.question: Why did Kwame and Adwoa’s first version of the app fail?
options: They coded without talking to users, making it data-heavy and confusing
Nobody in Accra ever needed a plumber or electrician
Their school computer had no keyboard
activities.explanation: Version 1 was built without customer discovery, so it wasted mobile data, failed on slow networks, and did not fit real users’ needs.

activities.definition: Protected in secret code so unauthorized people cannot read private data
distractors: Made to use extra mobile data on every click
Printed on street posters for strangers to read

activities.question: On a 100-cedi repair job, how was the payment split between the certified technician and the platform?
options: 90 cedis (90%) to the technician and 10 cedis (10%) platform fee
100 cedis to the app founders and 0 cedis to the technician
50 cedis to the customer and 50 cedis to the internet company
activities.explanation: The technician earned 90 cedis (90%) for their skilled work, while the 10-cedi (10%) fee covered servers, support, training and insurance.

activities.question: How did the platform reach 100 decent jobs after five years of steady work?
options: 25 full-time staff plus 75 certified technicians earning steady income
100 people downloading the app in the first five minutes
Hiring 100 actors to stand outside the bakery
activities.explanation: 25 full-time employees (engineers, support, inspectors, accountants) + 75 certified technicians = 100 jobs.

activities.prompt: Order the steps that turned Kwame and Adwoa’s failed prototype into a job-creating enterprise.
items: Interview real customers and technicians after Version 1 fails.
Build a low-data, private platform with certified technicians.
Grow over five years to support 25 staff and 75 technicians.
